items.stem: What type of correlation is shown when one variable tends to decrease as the other increases?
items.answer: Negative correlation
items.markingKey: Negative: as x increases, y tends to decrease.

items.stem: Explain the difference between strong and weak correlation.
items.answer: In strong correlation the points lie close to a straight line; in weak correlation there is a trend but the points are more spread out from the line.
items.markingKey: B1 strong: close to line; B1 weak: more scattered [2]

items.stem: Explain why it is useful to draw a scatter diagram before making predictions from data.
items.answer: It shows whether there is any correlation, how strong it is and whether there are outliers; predictions are only sensible if there is reasonable correlation.
items.markingKey: B1 shows correlation/strength; B1 outliers/whether prediction is sensible [2]

items.stem: The table shows the hours spent revising and the test mark (%) for a sample of 9. Hours spent revising: 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 13, 14. Test mark (%): 38, 28, 51, 54, 58, 65, 72, 86, 89. Calculate the mean of the hours spent revising and the mean of the test mark (%).
items.answer: mean x = 7.56, mean y = 60.11
items.markingKey: M1 sum ÷ 9 for each; A1 (7.56, 60.11).

items.stem: Data on the engine size (litres) and the fuel economy (km per litre) are collected. Engine size (litres): 1, 1.4, 1.6, 2.2, 2.9, 3.1, 3.3, 3.4, 3.7. Fuel economy (km per litre): 18.8, 17.2, 16.6, 14.3, 21, 13, 11.4, 11.5, 10.8. (a) Describe the correlation shown when the data are plotted. (b) Write down the coordinates of the point that is an outlier. (c) Calculate the coordinates of the mean point of all the data.
items.answer: (a) strong negative correlation (b) (2.9, 21) (c) (2.51, 14.96)
items.markingKey: (a) B1 strong negative correlation (b) B1 outlier (c) M1 mean of each; A1 (2.51, 14.96).

items.stem: Arjun records the age of a car (years) and the value of the car ($1000s) for a project in Muscat. Age of a car (years): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11. Value of the car ($1000s): 19, 17, 16, 17, 13, 12, 23, 7, 7, 6. (a) Ignoring the outlier, calculate the mean of each variable. (b) A line of best fit, drawn through the mean point and ignoring the outlier, has gradient −1.36. Use it to estimate the value of the car ($1000s) when the age of a car (years) is 8.
items.answer: (a) (5.67, 12.67) (b) 9.50 (accept a sensible value close to this)

items.stem: On a scatter diagram the points lie very close to a straight line sloping upwards. How is this correlation described?
items.answer: Strong positive
items.markingKey: Close to a line: strong; upward slope: positive.

items.stem: A scatter diagram of height against mass for a class shows positive correlation. Describe what this means in context.
items.answer: Taller students tend to be heavier.
items.markingKey: B1 in context, with "tend to" (not certainty) [2]

items.stem: Explain why one outlier should not be ignored without a reason.
items.answer: It could be a recording error, but it might be a genuine value; it should be checked before removing it from the analysis.
items.markingKey: B1 could be error; B1 could be genuine/check [2]

items.stem: Omar collects data in Dhaka on the daily hours of sunshine and the daily rainfall (mm). Daily hours of sunshine: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9. Daily rainfall (mm): 14.3, 16.4, 13.3, 13.6, 8.8, 8.6, 6.8, 5, 5.5. Describe the correlation and interpret it in context.
items.answer: Strong negative correlation: as the sunshine increases, the rainfall tends to decrease.
items.markingKey: B1 strong negative correlation; B1 interpretation in context [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain the difference between strong and weak correlation. (b) A scatter diagram of height against mass for a class shows positive correlation. Describe what this means in context.
items.answer: (a) In strong correlation the points lie close to a straight line; in weak correlation there is a trend but the points are more spread out from the line. (b) Taller students tend to be heavier.
items.markingKey: (a) B1 strong: close to line; B1 weak: more scattered [2] (b) B1 in context, with "tend to" (not certainty) [2]

items.stem: Mateo records the age of a car (years) and the value of the car ($1000s) for a project in Manila. Age of a car (years): 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 11. Value of the car ($1000s): 19, 18, 15, 29, 12, 10, 7, 5. (a) Identify the outlier and suggest one reason why it might have occurred. (b) Explain why using the line to estimate the value of the car ($1000s) when the age of a car (years) is 19 would not be reliable.
items.answer: (a) (5, 29); e.g. a recording error or an unusual day/person. (b) 19 is outside the range of the data (1 to 11), so this is extrapolation and the trend may not continue.
items.markingKey: (a) B1 point; B1 sensible reason [2] (b) B1 outside range; B1 extrapolation/trend may not continue [2]

items.stem: A line of best fit should pass through
items.answer: the mean point (x̄, ȳ)
items.markingKey: The mean point is a good balance point for the data.

items.stem: Explain why extrapolation can give unreliable estimates.
items.answer: The relationship has only been observed within the range of the data; outside it the trend may change, so the estimate may be wrong.
items.markingKey: B1 outside range of data; B1 trend may not continue [2]

items.stem: Explain why a line of best fit does not have to pass through the origin.
items.answer: It represents the trend of the data, which may not start at (0, 0); forcing it through the origin could misrepresent the data.
items.markingKey: B1 follows the data; B1 origin may not be meaningful [2]

items.stem: The equation of a line of best fit for the test mark (%) (y) against the hours spent revising (x) is y = 4.5x + 22. Use it to estimate the test mark (%) when the hours spent revising is 4.
items.markingKey: M1 substitute x = 4; A1 40.0.

items.stem: A line of best fit for the fuel economy (km per litre) (y) against the engine size (litres) (x) is y = −3.2x + 22. (a) Estimate the engine size when the fuel economy is 12.1. (b) Interpret the gradient of the line in context.
items.answer: (a) 3.09 (b) For each unit increase in engine size, the fuel economy decreases by about 3.20.
items.markingKey: (a) M1 12.1 = −3.2x + 22; A1 3.09 (b) B1 rate of change in context.

items.stem: Arjun records the hours spent revising and the test mark (%) for a project in Bogotá. Hours spent revising: 1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11. Test mark (%): 31, 23, 57, 54, 54, 64, 1, 78. (a) Ignoring the outlier, calculate the mean of each variable. (b) A line of best fit, drawn through the mean point and ignoring the outlier, has gradient 4.96. Use it to estimate the test mark (%) when the hours spent revising is 8.
items.answer: (a) (6.29, 51.57) (b) 60.1 (accept a sensible value close to this)
items.markingKey: (a) M1 sums ÷ number of values; A1 both [2] (b) M1 y − 51.57 = 4.96(x − 6.29); A1 60.1 [2]

items.stem: Using a line of best fit to estimate a value inside the range of the data is called
items.answer: interpolation
items.markingKey: Inside the range: interpolation; outside: extrapolation.

items.stem: Data were collected for values of x from 150 to 190. A line of best fit is used to estimate y when x = 130. Which statement is correct?
options: Interpolation, which is likely to be reliable
items.answer: Extrapolation, which may be unreliable
items.markingKey: x = 130 is outside 150 to 190.

items.stem: Explain why estimates from a line of best fit are more reliable when the correlation is strong.
items.answer: The points lie close to the line, so actual values are likely to be close to the values read from it.
items.markingKey: B1 points close to line; B1 smaller error [2]

items.stem: Explain why a line of best fit for weak correlation still gives only a rough estimate.
items.answer: The points are widely spread around the line, so individual values could differ a lot from the estimate.
items.markingKey: B1 wide spread; B1 rough estimate [2]

items.stem: Data on the distance from the city centre (km) and the monthly rent ($) were collected for values of the distance from centre between 1 and 18. The line of best fit is y = −42x + 1400. Sipho uses it to predict the monthly rent ($) when the distance from centre is 54, getting −868. Explain why this prediction may not be reliable.
items.answer: 54 is far outside the range of the data, so this is extrapolation; the trend may not continue (the value is not even realistic).
items.markingKey: B1 outside data range/extrapolation; B1 trend may not continue or value unrealistic [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why estimates from a line of best fit are more reliable when the correlation is strong. (b) Explain why a line of best fit for weak correlation still gives only a rough estimate.
items.answer: (a) The points lie close to the line, so actual values are likely to be close to the values read from it. (b) The points are widely spread around the line, so individual values could differ a lot from the estimate.
items.markingKey: (a) B1 points close to line; B1 smaller error [2] (b) B1 wide spread; B1 rough estimate [2]

items.stem: Samuel records the engine size (litres) and the fuel economy (km per litre) for a project in Kuala Lumpur. Engine size (litres): 1.4, 1.7, 2.3, 2.6, 2.8, 3.2, 3.4, 4. items.stem: Two variables show strong positive correlation. Which statement must be true?
options: One variable causes the other to increase
Higher values of one tend to go with higher values of the other
items.answer: Higher values of one tend to go with higher values of the other
items.markingKey: Correlation describes an association, not a cause.

items.stem: A third factor that affects both of two correlated variables is called
items.answer: a confounding (hidden) variable
items.markingKey: A hidden third variable can create a correlation without direct cause.

items.stem: Explain the difference between correlation and causation.
items.answer: Correlation means two variables tend to change together; causation means a change in one directly produces a change in the other. Correlation alone does not show causation.
items.markingKey: B1 correlation definition; B1 causation definition/distinction [2]

items.stem: A council in Muscat records, for 9 districts, an index of the number of mobile phones in a country (x) and of life expectancy (y). x: 12, 45, 47, 51, 55, 62, 80, 81, 89. y: 17, 34, 38, 44, 44, 43, 57, 62, 65. (a) Describe the correlation. (b) Calculate the mean point. (c) A councillor says reducing the number of mobile phones in a country would reduce life expectancy. Evaluate this claim.
items.answer: (a) strong positive correlation (b) (58, 44.89) (c) Not justified: correlation does not show causation; likely third factor — wealth of the country increases both.
items.markingKey: (a) B1 (b) M1 A1 (c) B1 correlation ≠ causation; B1 confounder named.

items.stem: Noah is investigating claims made in a newspaper in Riyadh. Midday temperature (°C): 16, 18, 20, 22, 25, 27, 29, 30, 31, 33. Number of cold drinks sold: 53, 75, 71, 89, 102, 120, 134, 145, 149, 164. (a) Describe the correlation in these data. (b) The newspaper also reports correlation between the number of fire engines sent to a fire and the amount of damage caused, and claims one causes the other. Explain why this is unlikely and suggest a third variable.
items.answer: (a) strong positive correlation (b) More likely a confounding variable: bigger fires need more engines and also cause more damage.
items.markingKey: (a) B1 [1] (b) B1 correlation ≠ causation; B1 third variable [2]

items.stem: Which statement about correlation and causation is correct?
options: Causation is impossible if there is correlation
items.answer: Correlation does not prove causation
items.markingKey: An association alone does not show that one variable changes the other.

items.stem: Data from Lisbon show positive correlation between the number of fire engines sent to a fire and the amount of damage caused. What is the most likely explanation?
options: There is no relationship of any kind
The amount of damage caused directly causes the number of fire engines sent to a fire to rise
A third factor: bigger fires need more engines and also cause more damage
The data must have been recorded incorrectly
items.answer: A third factor: bigger fires need more engines and also cause more damage
items.markingKey: This is a correlation caused by a confounding variable: bigger fires need more engines and also cause more damage.

items.stem: Explain why a scientist would carry out a controlled experiment rather than rely on a scatter diagram to show causation.
items.answer: In an experiment other variables can be kept the same, so any change can be linked to the variable being changed; a scatter diagram may reflect a hidden third variable.
items.markingKey: B1 control other variables; B1 rules out confounders [2]

items.stem: A report from Lima shows clear positive correlation between umbrellas sold and number of traffic accidents. Mei concludes that increasing umbrellas sold causes number of traffic accidents to increase. Explain why this conclusion may not be valid.
items.answer: Correlation does not prove causation; both are likely to be linked to a third factor (rainy weather increases both).
items.markingKey: B1 correlation ≠ causation; B1 identifies a plausible confounding factor [2]

items.stem: A council in Hanoi records, for 8 districts, an index of coffee shops in a district (x) and of average house price (y). x: 10, 21, 26, 56, 59, 66, 72, 87. y: 12, 23, 29, 47, 51, 50, 57, 70. (a) Describe the correlation. (b) Calculate the mean point. (c) A councillor says reducing coffee shops in a district would reduce average house price. Evaluate this claim.
items.answer: (a) strong positive correlation (b) (49.62, 42.38) (c) Not justified: correlation does not show causation; likely third factor — wealthier, busier districts have more of both.
items.markingKey: (a) B1 (b) M1 A1 (c) B1 correlation ≠ causation; B1 confounder named.

items.stem: Lucas is investigating claims made in a newspaper in Lisbon. Practice shots taken: 12, 13, 15, 23, 39, 41, 46, 51. Shots scored: 10, 11, 10, 15, 24, 26, 29, 32. (a) State whether you think a change in the practice shots could directly cause a change in the shots scored. Give a reason. (b) The newspaper also reports correlation between shoe size of children and reading ability, and claims one causes the other. Explain why this is unlikely and suggest a third variable.
items.answer: (a) A plausible direct link exists in this context, but the data alone cannot prove it. (b) More likely a confounding variable: older children have bigger feet and also read better.
items.markingKey: (a) B1 judgement; B1 reason referring to context [2] (b) B1 correlation ≠ causation; B1 third variable [2]

items.stem: Ethan is investigating claims made in a newspaper in Mumbai. Number of people in a household: 1.3, 2.1, 2.6, 2.7, 4, 5.2, 5.6, 6.6. (b) Suggest how a fair test could be designed to investigate whether one variable causes the other.
items.answer: (a) A plausible direct link exists in this context, but the data alone cannot prove it. (b) Change one variable while controlling all others (e.g. randomised groups), then compare the effect.
items.markingKey: (a) B1 judgement; B1 reason referring to context [2] (b) B1 control variables; B1 compare groups [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A scatter diagram of height against mass for a class shows positive correlation. Describe what this means in context. (b) Explain why it is useful to draw a scatter diagram before making predictions from data.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Two variables show strong positive correlation. Which statement must be true? (b) Which situation is most likely to be a genuine cause-and-effect relationship?

items.stem: Explain why a correlation found in a small sample may be misleading.
items.answer: With few data points a pattern can happen by chance or be caused by one or two unusual values, so it may not hold for the whole population.

items.stem: A report from Manila shows weak positive correlation between ice cream sales and the number of people who get sunburnt. Isla concludes that increasing ice cream sales causes the number of people who get sunburnt to increase. Explain why this conclusion may not be valid.
